notes.title: Creator Spotlight : Alexandre Zenga - Lead Level Designer
notes.content:
[p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/f29adfebcc015bf4fde11c834b797bbb3ab3adfa.png"][/img][/p][p][b][i]Hell is Us[/i] is now out and we hope you are enjoying the game! On our end, we're going to keep unveiling the work and minds of some of the creators behind the game in our Creator Spotlight series of articles.

Today, we chat with Alexandre Zenga, Lead Level Designer on [i]Hell is Us[/i]!

Can you tell us about your journey as a video game developer and how you came to be working on Hell is Us as lead level designer?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]From my younger years playing the old classics as a kid all the way up to the big blockbusters we see today, I’ve always been captivated and amazed by video games. Back in the day, like many young boys of my age, I had no idea what I wanted to do with my life and video games were my passion and my refuge. [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]As a young adult in the mid 2000’s, I learned about a newly created school right here in my hometown of Montréal, that was specialized with video game specific programs called Campus Ubisoft at the time (now Campus ADN). That was my calling! I applied to their Level Design class and got selected. [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]After a few years of experience in the industry, I joined Funcom in 2010 where I met Bruno Parenteau (Game Director) a fellow Gameplay Designer then, and we quickly became friends. After the release of The Secret World and the unfortunate fate of Funcom Montréal, Bruno joined his long-time friend Yves Bordeleau (CEO) at his new studio which became [b]Rogue Factor[/b]. In 2013, during the early stage of development of [b][i]Mordheim: City of the Damned[/i][/b], Yves and Bruno quickly realized they needed a Level Designer on the team, and they recruited me. [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]Fast forward over the years, we shipped [b][i]Mordheim: City of the Damned, Necromunda: Underhive Wars[/i][/b] and Jonathan Jacques-Belletête (Creative Director) joined us. After the team grew up in size and strength, I was offered the opportunity, and the honor, to become the Lead Level Designer on [b][i]Hell is Us[/i][/b][i].[/i][/p][p align="justify"] [img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/49e2d28dc4ed301ae714f97af40995bc78dc3dda.jpg"][/img][/p][p][b]Considering the player-plattering philosophy of Hell is Us (no quest markers, no map, etc), how do you find the balance between letting the player figure things out by himself and not being too obtuse and thus frustrate the player?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]That was a real challenge! While we wanted to give enough information to the player, we didn’t want it to be too “on the nose” either, it wouldn’t have felt natural. We had to adjust the dosage depending on what type of content we were working on, especially the main storyline. We were very meticulous with our landmarks placement and made sure they were visible enough. We don’t want you to feel lost, but we also want you to have those “Eureka!” moments that feels great when you figure something out. [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]Some secrets are hidden in plain sight, while others are so deeply hidden, you may only discover them in a subsequent playthrough. It was very fun to implement. We even had our own internal difficulty scale for those secrets, it went like this: easy, medium, hard and “must go on Reddit”. We hope you have as much fun uncovering them as we had designing them. Good luck! [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/7d8f6b9db85b6e293a45b0237f04bb41eac93ec7.jpg"][/img][/p][p][b]Hell is Us features both open zones and dungeons. What were the specific challenges that you faced in designing these types of locations?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]Both had to feel different but still needed to follow the design principles and core pillars of [b][i]Hell is Us.[/i][/b] Generally speaking, open zones have more freedom of exploration while dungeons are a little more linear. We wanted to keep some of that “open zone freedom” in our dungeon designs and add some linearity in our open zone designs, all while keeping the principle of player-plattering. So, you might have a different experience from your friends who are playing the game because you made different choices, or you completed parts of the game in a different order. [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/e4c62904a330707b3b644d27fe4f134a3da21b99.jpg"][/img][/p][p][b]Rogue Factor’s previous projects were tactical role-playing games; what is the biggest challenge in transitioning to a 3rd person action-adventure game?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]In [b][i]Hell is Us[/i][/b], our map designs are a lot more oriented on exploration, immersion and experience rather than on tactics, vantage and choke points. While balanced and tactical maps are fun to design, it was a breath of fresh air after several years on a different genre. When we first transitioned from [b][i]Necromunda[/i][/b], everything we made was way too large in scale and vastly open because we were used to the environments of that universe. Additionally, Hell is Us’ controls are very different and with the combat system being focused on melee, so we had to completely review how we built maps. [/p][p] [/p][p][b]Where do you look for inspiration? Video games, other media, real-world locations?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]Honestly, all of the above and then some... We look for inspiration everywhere we can! Some areas of the game are heavily inspired from cult video game moments while other areas are based on real-world locations, but nothing hits the spot as much as seeing the work of our own artists. When I see a new concept art or the work of our environment artists, it really triggers something special! [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/7008a53ee95ad22ef7d05e058de7287a5dd6c074.jpg"][/img][/p][p][b]What kind of a gamer are you? Is there a game you always go back to?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]I'm a hardcore gamer and a huge fan of RPG, MMORPG, Action RPG, Hack & Slash, Roguelikes and Incremental Games. I will always be a min-maxer, I absolutely thrive on pushing the limits of power in games. There are a couple games that will always have a special place in my heart: [b][i]EverQuest[/i][/b], which I have incredibly fond memories of, and [b][i]Path of Exile[/i][/b] is the game that keeps bringing me back for more regularly. Shout out to my friends on The Tower, you guys are amazing! [/p][p] [/p][p][b]In your whole career, what are you most proud of?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]The team and the studio we built at Rogue Factor, without a doubt. I know this sounds cliché, but it’s true. When I first joined, we were just a dozen of devs with a lot of ambition. We grew together over the years, aged together, developed unparalleled comraderies and relationships, increased our expertise and recruited incredible talents on the team. This is what makes Rogue Factor so special for me today and I’m incredibly proud of our achievements. [/p]

notes.title: All Hell is Us Good Deeds and how to complete them
notes.content:
How do you complete all Good Deeds in Hell is Us? Hadea isn't too friendly to outsiders, but if you want to get on someone's good side, then doing them a solid is a good place to start. Good Deeds are optional side quests that often involve going out of your way to return a specific item, but with Rogue Factor's hands-off approach to exploration, finding those items is easier said than done.

There are 23 Good Deeds in Hell is Us, and some are more straightforward than others. A few even have hidden time restrictions and parameters that make it possible to fail, which can have dire consequences for the NPCs you're trying to help in the action-adventure game. However, the rewards are well worth it, especially if you're looking for the best Glyphs for your build.

notes.title: Hell Is Us (PC) Review
notes.content:
Hell Is Us is an atypical action-adventure game that embraces old-school design philosophies in a modern light, creating a unique and hauntingly dark slow burn of an experience.

As a massive fan of the Deus Ex reboot games, I was thrilled to find out that Hell Us‘s art direction has Jonathan Jacques-Belletête at the helm as the Creative Director and art lead for the game, the same person responsible for bringing Deus Ex to life. Instead of a futuristic mechanized world, Hell is Us takes place in the 90s and features a grounded aesthetic juxtaposed with unearthly entities called Hollow Walkers that look akin to contemporary surrealist statutes come to life.

Leveraging the power of Unreal Engine 5, Hell is Us is an often gorgeous game set in the fictional country of Hadea. notes.title: Creator Spotlight : Mathieu Larivière - Lead Writer
notes.content:
[p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/812378184240e97921c13e488554c5a4908bb0a6.png"][/img][b]

First of all, can you tell us about your journey as a game developer and how you did yourself working at Rogue Factor as the lead writer of Hell is Us?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p][i]I started my career as a game designer at a small company called Microids Canada. Like many indie studios, it was a place where you wore multiple hats, which turned out to be an incredible learning experience. I was exposed to nearly every part of development, and that breadth of responsibility helped me build a strong foundation. My first true writing experience came while working on a small adventure game called Still Life, where I served as both lead designer and writer.[/i] [/p][p][/p][p][i]After seven years at Microids, I transitioned into the world of triple-A, first with Ubisoft and then later at Eidos Montreal. At Ubisoft, I continued as a game designer, but it was at Eidos where I made a definitive shift into writing. I took on the role of narrative designer and realized very quickly that writing, not design, was where I belonged. It felt like a much more natural fit. Even outside of work, I was always writing screenplays, worldbuilding, and characters, so making that switch professionally just made sense.[/i] [/p][p][/p][p][i]Eventually, after several years in the big studio system, I joined Rogue Factor, a smaller studio that was starting work on a fascinating new project. It felt like the right time to return to a more agile environment where creative voices could be heard clearly, and where I could bring everything I’d learned to a role focused entirely on narrative.[/i] [/p][p][/p][p][i]Joining Rogue Factor as the lead writer on Hell is Us was a return to form. It was the first time I felt that level of creative trust from day one. I wasn’t just brought in to “write the words”. I was part of shaping the world, the lore, the characters, and the narrative systems themselves. It was a long project, and like any long project, there were highs and lows. But the level of collaboration across departments, the openness to dialogue, and the shared belief in the game we were creating made it deeply rewarding.[/i] [/p][p][/p][p][i]Hell is Us challenged me, stretched me, and gave me space to grow, not just as a writer, but as a creative partner. It’s a project I’m proud of, not only for what we built on screen, but for how we built it behind the scenes.[/i] [/p][p]  [/p][p][b]Hell is Us is a pretty dark game in terms of setting and themes. Hadea being in a middle of a vicious civil war; there are of course themes of genocide, religious conflict, war crimes, propaganda, etc. [/b]  [/p][p][b]Did you research specific historical events?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p][i]Yes, absolutely. You can’t write about civil war, systemic violence, or propaganda without grounding yourself in the real-world history of those things. While Hell is Us is a fictional world, many of the themes are genocide, occupation, repression, and information warfare. They are drawn from patterns we’ve seen repeated throughout history.[/i] 

[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/68689c04b99a35e9a99b8733b638f2ea2a0ef7ea.png"][/img][/p][p] [/p][p][i]I didn’t focus on one single historical event, but instead cast a wide net across different conflicts and periods: the American Civil War, the French Revolution, Yugoslavia in the 1990s, Rwanda in the 1990s, occupied France during WWII, and even more recent global events. It wasn’t about replicating any one situation, but understanding the mechanisms: how societies break down, how ideologies harden, how people justify the unjustifiable.[/i] [/p][p] [/p][p]That context gave depth to the world of Hadea, and, hopefully, gave players something to think about beyond just the gameplay. [/p][p][/p][p][b]Was it hard to address themes that have been so present in current world events?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p][i]Yes, and it should be hard. You don’t write about war crimes, genocide, or authoritarian regimes lightly, especially when echoes of those realities are happening right now. There were moments where it hit a little too close to home, when real-world headlines mirrored the themes we were writing about. [/i][/p][p][i] [/i][/p][p][i]That said, the goal was never to exploit those themes for shock value. It was about using fiction to explore the emotional and psychological weight of those experiences, and to ask: What happens to people living in broken systems? How do they adapt, justify, survive, or resist? [/i][/p][p][i] [/i][/p][p][i]I think the challenge is to approach that material with humility. You’re not trying to provide answers—you’re creating space for reflection, tension, and ambiguity. And if any of that sticks with the player after they put the controller down, then I think we’ve done our job.[/i][/p][p][/p][p][b]What do you do when you need to take your mind off these themes?[/b] [/p][p] [/p][p][i]Honestly, you have to. When you’re spending months immersed in subject matter like war, trauma, and human cruelty, you need a way to come up for air. For me, it’s usually about switching gears, reading fiction that has nothing to do with darkness or violence, playing games that are purely about joy or exploration (Stellar Blade and an absurd amount of The First Descendant), spending time with friends and family, or just walking the dogs to reset. [/i][/p][p][i] [/i][/p][p][i]Writing something heavy doesn’t mean you have to live in that emotional space 24/7. I think stepping away once in a while helps you write it better, with more perspective, more balance, and more humanity. The worst thing you can do is let the darkness numb you.[/i] [/p][p][/p][p][b]Hell is Us has also a lot of science-fiction, even fantastical, elements. What was your approach to organically combine the socio-political themes and the sci-fi parts?[/b] [/p][p] [/p][p][i]The key was to make sure the science-fiction elements didn’t feel like an escape hatch, but a lens, something that amplified the real-world themes rather than distracting from them. For me, the fantastical parts of Hell is Us were never there just for spectacle. They were metaphorical, symbolic. The Calamity and the Hollow Walkers, for instance, aren’t just monsters. They’re manifestations of human emotions. 

[/i][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/108b42ce0c9c2580d4acfcf07bed2bb994ad5100.png"][/img][/p][p][i] [/i][/p][p][i]The idea was to take real socio-political issues like the civil war, genocide, propaganda, and filter them through a speculative world that lets us explore them in a heightened, sometimes surreal way. That gives the player enough distance to reflect, but not so much distance that the emotional weight is lost. [/i][/p][p][i] [/i][/p][p][i]In short, the sci-fi parts aren’t a departure from the political themes. They’re an extension of them. They let us go deeper by making the invisible visible.[/i] [/p][p][/p][p][b]When looking for inspiration, where do you look for it? Other games, movies, books? Are there specific works, documentary or fiction, that inspired your writing in Hell is Us?[/b]  
 [/p][p][i]I[/i] [i]cast a wide net when it comes to inspiration. Of course, I look at games, but also books, films, documentaries, even music or visual art. Sometimes a mood or tone from a photograph or a melody can say more than a thousand words. [/i][/p][p][/p][p][i]For Hell is Us, I was particularly drawn to works that explore broken societies and existential conflict. I revisited war documentaries, read historical accounts of civil unrest and regime collapse, and looked at fiction that delves into the psychological weight of violence and authoritarianism. Orwell was a key influence, 1984 in particular, for its unflinching portrayal of manipulation, control, and the fragility of truth. That novel continues to resonate, especially in a world where information is increasingly weaponized. [/i][/p][p][/p][p][i]I also looked at films like Children of Men, Fury, and No Man’s Land. Not because we were trying to imitate them, but because they showed how you can tackle bleak, complex subjects with honesty and restraint.[/i][/p][p][/p][p][i]In terms of games, titles like Spec Ops: The Line (inspired by Heart of Darkness), Bloodborne, and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. stood out. They’re not afraid to be uncomfortable or ambiguous, and they trust the player to engage with something more profound. For me, inspiration isn’t about borrowing.  It’s about asking, Why did this resonate? What emotional truth did it tap into? And then finding your answer to that through the world you’re building. [/i][/p][p] [/p][p][b]Now for some more fun questions:[/b]  [/p][p][b]In your career, what are you the most proud of?[/b] [/p][p] [/p][p]I’d have to say [i]Still Life[/i], even though I cringe a little every time I look back at it. It was the first project where I created everything from scratch: the story, the world, the characters, the tone. It was raw, imperfect, and very much a product of its time, but it was mine. And despite all its flaws, it still holds a special place as the best thing I’ve ever done. You never really forget your first full creative leap like that. [/p][p] [/p][p]A very close second would be [i]Hell is Us[/i]. It was a different kind of pride, more mature, more collaborative. I had the chance to work with an incredibly talented team, and together we tackled some complex, weighty themes. It was the first time I had that level of narrative ownership on a large-scale game, and I’m proud of the risks we took and the emotional depth we reached. [/p][p] 
[b]What do you think is the best written game of all-time?[/b]  [/p][p] [/p][p]That’s a brutal question. I’d have to go with a three-way tie between [i]Bloodborne[/i], [i]The Last of Us[/i], and [i]Bioshock[/i]. [/p][p] [/p][p][i]Bloodborne[/i] is a masterclass in atmospheric storytelling. It trusts the player to work for the narrative, to uncover its dense lore through item descriptions, cryptic dialogue, and world design. There’s almost no fat in the writing. It’s sharp, unsettling, and minimalist in the best way. [/p][p] [/p][p][i]The Last of Us[/i] sits on the other end of the spectrum: structured, emotional, and deeply character-driven. The relationship between Joel and Ellie is full of tension, conflict, and quiet moments of vulnerability. The way the story ties into gameplay mechanics, pacing, and emotional payoff, especially that ending, is still unmatched. [/p][p] [/p][p]And then there’s [i]Bioshock[/i]. That game floored me when I first played it. Its integration of philosophy, player agency, and narrative design was groundbreaking. The world of Rapture, the use of unreliable narration, and the twist showed just how smart and subversive game writing could be. [/p][p] [/p][p]Each of these games approaches storytelling differently, but all three left a lasting impression and pushed the boundaries of what narrative in games can do. [/p][p] 
 [b]What kind of gamer are you? Is there a game that you always go back to?[/b]  [/p][p] [/p][p]I used to be the kind of gamer who played one game and played it hard. [i]World of Warcraft[/i] was my go-to for years. It had this way of pulling you in completely, and before I knew it, I’d spent a huge chunk of my gaming time inside Azeroth. I quit about two years ago, and since then, it’s felt like I’ve been playing catch-up with everything I missed. [/p][p] [/p][p]These days, I’m drawn to the Eastern gaming experience. There’s something compelling about the aesthetics, tone, and pacing in games like [i]Black Myth: Wukong[/i], [i]Wuchang: Fallen Feathers[/i], [i]Stellar Blade[/i], [i]The First Descendant[/i], and the upcoming [i]Tides of Annihilation[/i]. They blend precision, beauty, and worldbuilding in a way that clicks with me. [/p][p] [/p][p]So, I guess now I’d say I’m an explorer. I want to see what other developers and cultures are doing with storytelling and design. I’m still catching up, but I’m enjoying every minute of it. [/p][p] [/p]

notes.title: Creator spotlight : Stéphane Primeau - composer
notes.content:
[p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/1313e51116917c7dd46bee7e16f2334c3820c610.png"][/img][b]

First of all, tell us a little bit about your journey as a musician and how you came about on working with Rogue Factor on [i]Hell is Us[/i]?[/b] 
[/p][p]I started learning music at a fairly young age. I was fortunate to attend a school specialized in classical music, where we learned ensemble music, singing, piano, violin, and more. We were later given the choice to continue with either the violin or the piano. I chose the piano at that time. I continued taking lessons until the end of high school. Meanwhile, I played drums in a few small music groups.  [/p][p][/p][p]It was only a bit later that I joined the band [b]Unexpect[/b], where I initially played drums, but eventually returned to piano and keyboard, which is my main instrument. The band grew in popularity, allowing us to go on several international tours.  [/p][p][/p][p]It was during those times that I met Yves Bordeleau (CEO of [b]Rogue Factor[/b]), as we performed together with our respective bands. He already had a video game company back then, and since I enjoyed composing that kind of music at home for fun, I eventually ended up working for him. I left [b]Unexpect[/b] after a great tour with Dream Theater in 2009, which allowed me to fully focus on composing video game soundtracks. [/p][p] [/p][p][i][b]Hell is Us[/b][/i][b] deals with some dark themes as the country of Hadea is in a middle of a vicious civil war. Also, extreme emotions like rage, grief, terror and ecstasy are intertwined in the game’s lore. What is your process to translate these themes and settings into music?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p]I did a lot of sound research for [i][b]Hell is Us[/b][/i]. My goal was to find very specific sonic textures to make the player feel tension and oppression during exploration, without necessarily falling into pure horror. All of this was blended with mystery and intrigue to highlight the investigative aspect of the game.[/p][p] [/p][p]I allowed myself quite a bit of freedom when it came to the emotional side of the music. Even though we define specific emotions with names, to me, emotions are almost always uncontrollable—or at least, we don’t really choose when they arise. That’s the approach I took with the sound design for the music. I wanted to create strange, unconventional sounds with expression and dynamics. That’s the beauty of music when you let it guide you through unpredictability and experimentation. [/p][p][/p][previewyoutube="k1IoRwvsbao;full"][/previewyoutube][p] [/p][p][b]When looking for inspiration, where do you look for it? Other games, movies, your old records? Is there a specific inspiration for your work in Hell is Us? [/b] [/p][p][/p][p]For [i][b]Hell is Us[/b],[/i] several references were suggested to me, such as the films [i][b]Annihilation[/b][/i],[b] [i]Alien[/i][/b], [i][b]Interstellar[/b][/i], etc. Personally, the TV series [i][b]Dark[/b][/i] also inspired me with its intimate and strange atmosphere. I try as much as possible to keep certain influences on the surface, but I like to forget them once my composition process is fully underway, in order to be as original as possible. [/p][p] [/p][p][b]Is there a piece in the game that you are particularly proud of and that players should look forward to?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p]The Intro Credits track. After seeing the early work done on this cinematic, I felt it needed a TV series-style opening piece—something that broke away from the usual ambient mold, with a more forward and present sound, especially since the music was created before the cinematic itself. I had complete creative freedom to do what I wanted while highlighting the game’s themes. [/p][p] [/p][p][b]What is your favorite piece of music of all-time that you’ve heard in a video game?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p]I don’t really have a favorite track. I’m someone who listens to a wide variety of musical styles, and many pieces impress me. If I had to choose, I’d say the music from the [i][b]Final Fantasy VII Remake[/b][/i]. There are some incredible tracks in there. [/p][p] [/p][p][b]How much of a gamer are you and is there a game that you always go back to?[/b] [/p][p][/p][p]I've always been a gamer. I'm from the generation that started out playing on old retro devices like the Intellivision or the Commodore 64. I'm more into solo adventures, RPGs, and puzzles. I really enjoy games with a strong story and a surrounding mystery. I'm not much of an online gamer, except maybe for [i][b]Fallout 76[/b][/i] (I'm a big fan of the Fallout series). I also like to finish one game at a time to fully enjoy it. There are only two games I've played twice, but those are exceptions: the [i][b]Mass Effect[/b][/i] series and [i][b]The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past.[/b][/i] [/p]

notes.title: The Evolution of Rogue Factor : Small Team, Big Ideas, Rogue Hearts
notes.content:
[p align="justify"][b]How it’s going :[/b] [/p][p align="justify"]It’s 2025; Rogue Factor’s CEO Yves Bordeleau is at Gamescom in Germany to promote the upcoming release of [b][i]Hell is Us.[/i][/b] 
[/p][p align="justify"][b]How it started : [/b] [/p][p align="justify"]It was 2013; Rogue Factor’s CEO Yves Bordeleau was at Gamescom in Germany, carrying under his arm a prototype of a tactical strategy video game set in the [b]Warhammer[/b] universe. [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]Leveraging his vast network of friends in the industry, Yves Bordeleau managed to secure a meeting with senior executives at Games Workshop to show them a proof of concept of what would become [b][i]Mordheim: City of the Damned[/i][/b] [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/131e577eda0541a643524b4effc0b3f80aaab290.jpg"][/img]                                                              [i]The first Rogue Factor offices[/i][/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]This demo was developed by a small group of enthusiastic developers who were fans of the iconic tabletop game.  [/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]The catch?[/p][p][/p][p align="justify"]They didn’t [b]yet[/b] have the rights to the license!  [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]Bold and risky, but that’s how Rogues roll, right? [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]As you’ve probably guessed, the reason we’re telling you this story is because he pulled it off. [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]The Games Workshop executives were impressed and agreed to let this small team of passionate Quebecers develop an official Warhammer video game—from their modest offices in the working-class neighborhood of Hochelaga in Montreal. [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]And that’s how Rogue Factor was born. Rogue not just in name, but in spirit. [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/9b236d0fa7848e894100eb32d66e43825dcfdedf.jpg"][/img]                                                                    [i]Team Mordheim![/i][/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"][b][i]Mordheim: City of the Damned[/i][/b] was developed by a team of around 20 devs. [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]Later, the team grew to around 30 developers during the development of [b][i]Necromunda: Underhive Wars[/i][/b], a second game under the Warhammer license. [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]In 2018, Yves Bordeleau and his band of rogues caught the attention of French publisher Nacon, who acquired the studio in a deal that comprised sister studios Cyanide and Big Bad Wolf as well. [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/878c9d4a141e97845335ac896c2d16dd73b59099.jpg"][/img]                                    [i]Rogue Factor's offices during the developement of Necromunda[/i][/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]A year later, Jonathan Jacques-Belletête—known for being the Executive Art Director of the [b][i]Deus Ex[/i][/b] titles at Eidos Montreal, and fresh off his work as Art director on [b][i]Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy[/i][/b]—joined Rogue Factor. [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]The rebellious spirit of Yves Bordeleau and the unique creative vision of Jonathan Jacques-Belletête came together to redefine Rogue Factor. [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/9f46b10a6df819a7417de3a8271d9bff0733bcfc.png"][/img]                                   [i]Jonathan Jacques-Belletête (left) and Yves Bordeleau (right)[/i][/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]How does Rogue Factor position itself in the ever-changing landscape of the video game industry? They had this idea of making Rogue Factor a[b] « boutique[/b] [b]studio »[/b] : Making games differently—somewhere between a AAA studio and a small indie team—with a core of veterans eager to stand out in an increasingly formulaic industry. [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]A new motto emerged as their creative driving philosophy : [b]Design distinctions create desire.[/b] [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"][b][i]Hell is Us[/i][/b] is the embodiment of all that. [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]A project that could have easily gone off the rails, as most of its development took place during the COVID-19 pandemic. But through resilience, leadership, creative talent and technical know-how, the team adapted—without compromising on quality and without compromising on working conditions. [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]In 2024, the team moved to brand new offices in the Mile-End neighborhood, known as the artistic heart of Montreal and home to its world-renowned bagels! Rogue Factor is now neighbor to many video game studios, from AAAs to indies. [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/a2f1239179982f36120051e7f85cc0e790439b50.jpg"][/img]                          [i]The current offices of Rogue Factor in the Mile-End neighbordhood in Montreal[/i][/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]Today, the studio has 60 employees, with a team of 50 who developed [b][i]Hell is Us[/i][/b]. [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]Aside from Nacon’s tremendous support in marketing, localization, and a bit of QA, everything on [b][i]Hell is Us[/i][/b] was done in-house. The English and French voice casts are mostly Quebec-based and were recorded in Rogue Factor’s own sound booths. The music was also composed internally. Even the motion capture sessions were all done in Rogue Factor’s studio. [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/79d83b88859e8c443aa94dc97a9dee5cf4367e49.jpg"][/img]                                                               [i]Rogue Factor in 2025[/i][/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"][i]Hell is Us[/i] is a game developed over five years by a human-sized team, driven by a unique creative vision. [/p][p align="justify"][/p][p align="justify"]We can’t wait to see you play it. [/p]

notes.title: French cast spotlight

He is the official French-Canadian voice of actor Tom Hardy and has also been heard in Hollywood films such as [i]Guardians of the Galaxy[/i], [i]Pirates of the Caribbean[/i], and [i]Harry Potter[/i], among others.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/d9752ad3a28d6eedbb5b0a99c7123be3f6dd178d.jpg"][/img][/p][p]You’ll also hear in [b][i]Hell is Us[/i][/b] the voices of Noémie Godin-Vigneault ([b][i]Stat[/i][/b]), Eric Paulhus ([b][i]Indéfendable[/i][/b]), Mylène Saint-Sauveur ([b][i]Alerte Amber[/i][/b]), Paul Ahmarani ([b][i]La moitié gauche du frigo[/i][/b]), Jean-Philippe Baril Guérard ([b][i]Mouvement Deluxe[/i][/b]), and many others.[/p][p][/p][p][url="https://steamcommunity.com/games/1620730/announcements/detail/515217056009814542?snr=2"]The english cast[/url] also features many Québécois and Canadian actors.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/d8c9952ad48e7ad40f9a96a12ae1de33160cb674.jpg"][/img][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/70e97e40704435762b4a2ccdac517fb1304bb0f0.jpg"][/img][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/f7e71d7a9ab8df06da23dabdea1b64abd7acd9de.jpg"][/img][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/067da9b8b015082b59f1293297bc2e71969961c6.jpg"][/img][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/c044d6b7d28cb91aed0cdd739eaaa04465a2c6ba.jpg"][/img][/p]

notes.title: Spotlight on the english cast
notes.content:
[p][b][i]Hell is Us[/i][/b] features captivating exploration and discovery, exciting combat, elaborate dungeons and puzzles, as well as countless secrets. All these fundamental elements are intricately woven together thanks to the emotional odyssey at the heart of the game: Remi’s journey. 
[/p][p]As we travel through Hadea, we encounter allies, enemies, and ordinary Hadeans simply trying to survive a brutal civil war—with all the deep physical and psychological wounds that come with it. 
[/p][p]To convey this emotional range, Rogue Factor brought together a talented and diverse cast of voice actors you may have already seen or heard in your favorite films, TV shows, or video games. 
[/p][p]Here is English voice cast of [b][i]Hell is Us[/i][/b][i].[/i] [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/cf91793e1bd6991f589a68e5cb3c0b0dc372108f.jpg"][/img][/p][p][b]Elias Toufexis (Remi)[/b] 
[/p][p]If you’re a gamer, chances are you’ve already heard his voice. Montreal-born Elias Toufexis is best known as the voice of Adam Jensen in [b][i]Deus Ex: Human Revolution[/i][/b] and [b][i]Deus Ex: Mankind Divided[/i].[/b] 
[/p][p]You’ve also seen him on screen in sci-fi series like [b][i]The Expanse[/i][/b], where he played Kenzo, and [b][i]Star Trek: Discovery[/i][/b], where he portrayed L'ak, a member of the Breen species. Although the Breen were first introduced in [i]Star Trek: The Original Series[/i] in the 1960s, Elias Toufexis is the first actor in the franchise’s history to show the face of a Breen! 
[/p][p]You’ve also heard his voice in video game franchises such as [b][i]Dynasty Warriors[/i], [i]Starfield[/i], [i]Death Stranding[/i][/b], and[b] [i]Fallout[/i][/b], among many others. [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/e2943581099beec1a7525e9587503e62fc71e1de.jpg"][/img][/p][p][b]Patricia Summersett[/b] 
[/p][p]None other than Princess Zelda herself! Yes, the Canadian actress lends her voice to the Hylian princess in [b][i]The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild[/i][/b] and [b][i]The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom[/i].[/b] 
[/p][p]In addition to her work in major franchises like [b][i]Assassin’s Creed[/i], [i]Far Cry[/i], and [i]Star Wars Outlaws[/i][/b], she has also appeared on the big screen, notably in [b][i]Mother![/i][/b] by legendary director Darren Aronofsky. 
[/p][p]On television, you may have seen her in [b][i]Star Trek: Discovery[/i][/b] (also playing a Breen) and[b] [i]Three Pines[/i][/b], among others. [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/bb161be29ab5bbd60ac310e5651be60882b0e088.jpg"][/img][/p][p][b]Caroline Dhavernas[/b] 
[/p][p]Caroline Dhavernas is a Montreal-born actress who has found success in both French- and English-language television and film. She is best known for her roles as Jaye Tyler in [b][i]Wonderfalls[/i][/b] and Alana Bloom in [b][i]Hannibal[/i][/b], for which she received a Saturn Award nomination. 
[/p][p]Her career began at a young age in Quebec, with numerous roles in children’s and teen shows, followed by appearances in films such as [b][i]Fathers and Guns[/i][/b] and [b][i]Hochelaga, Land of Souls[/i][/b]. In the world of video games, you’ve heard her as the narrator in [b][i]Child of Light[/i][/b] and as Theodrate in [b][i]Assassin’s Creed: Valhalla[/i].[/b] [/p][p][/p][p][b]Hell is us also features the voices of :[/b] [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/4e26f32e5ff4ef267647a7d5b5f4ea34884e6394.jpg"][/img][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/125d9efabdb1b737a84a973ce0518ef37dc07886.jpg"][/img][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/6618e9842891b9ed4ca76ff606d75cc4e752b869.jpg"][/img][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/e675b098965121ce789ab4d6606b3639438a706a.jpg"][/img][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/dd2c567cbd5223ec30d229f3dfbc5754dee888b1.jpg"][/img][/p]

notes.title: HELL IS US – New Demo Patch Notes
notes.content:
[p][b]The Hell is Us demo is back! It will be available at 3 PM CEST / 6 AM PT.[/b][/p][p]
Months after its first appearance, the demo returns — now enhanced with new features, quality-of-life improvements, and refined gameplay to make your return to Hadea even smoother. notes.title: Carve your own path
notes.content:
[p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/c98a3faf115cef20a6ff248bad9a17e95a629fc3.png"][/img][i]

Hell is Us[/i] doesn’t follow the usual rules.[/p][p]There’s no glowing quest marker. No checklist of objectives guiding you from point A to B. The game highlights what truly matters — but only through the world itself. It’s up to you to connect the dots.

[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/da00cf62fe11734186974540fa29b4004306733c.jpg"][/img][/p][p]Rather than following a rigid path, [i]Hell is Us[/i] gives you the space to choose when[b] [/b]you approach its challenges. At key moments, you're given multiple directions to explore, and it's up to you to decide which patch draws your curiosity. Progression is flexible. And that flexibility gives every player a chance to shape their own experience.[/p][p]That freedom also extends beyond the main story.[/p][p]If you want to stay focused on your primary objective, you can. But you might also come across a secluded vault, a disturbing relic, or a mysterious request for help. Will you stop to investigate? Will you intervene? Or will you walk away, unsure of what you’ve just witnessed?

[img src="data:image/jpeg;base64,"][/img][/p][p] [/p][p]There are no traditional fetch quests here. No filler. No "go here, do this" just to pad your journey. Every side encounter — whether it’s an act of kindness, a hidden space to uncover, or an eerie sign of something deeper — exists for a reason. You won’t find quest logs or clear rewards. What you take from them depends entirely on you.[/p][p]In [i]Hell is Us[/i], nothing is meaningless — not even what you choose to ignore.[/p]

notes.title: The weapons in Hell is Us
notes.content: [p][i][b]Hell is Us[/b][/i] [b]takes place in 1993 in the fictional country of Hadea, where a vicious civil war is still raging when the protagonist, Remi, arrives.[/b] [/p][p][/p][p]Although it's the 20th century, all combat in the game is carried out using medieval-style melee weapons. Why?  [/p][p]  [/p][p]These weapons are not forged from ordinary metal and they seem to be the only weapons that can hurt the mysterious entities that have suddenly invaded Hadea. Like the mystery of the Calamity, the weapons are clearly very ancient...  [/p][p]  [/p][p][b]Where do they come from?[/b]  [/p][p]  [/p][p][b]Who created them, and why?[/b]  [/p][p]  [/p][p][b]Why are the creatures vulnerable to them?[/b]  [/p][p]  [/p][p]These are mysteries you’ll be able to uncover during your adventures in Hadea! [/p][p][/p][p]While you wait to wield them, here's some [b]concept art[/b] for the weapons in Hell is Us : [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/c1b2c7093a8a9c31f54357432a93b2e26f1140ca.jpg"][/img][/p][p]And a few screenshots of them [b]in action[/b] :[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/873a249cf3c58d2e3c651b2fdc4a233a64e5f951.jpg"][/img][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/a04ec8cf2094e408fa759481b7c8841f5ca44017.jpg"][/img][/p]

notes.title: Community Update #2 – Press Tour, demo and more
notes.content:
[p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/1f723e6a1c29951e1435594771c14aeb03dec8fe.jpg"][/img]

Hello, community![/p][p]In our [url="https://steamcommunity.com/games/1620730/announcements/detail/515209445812209435?snr=2___"]first community update[/url], we gave you a summary of everything that had been publicly released about [i]Hell is Us[/i] over the past year.[/p][p]Now that we’re approaching the release date of [b]September 4, 2025[/b] (just three months away!), communications are ramping up, and you’ll be hearing more and more about [i]Hell is Us[/i]—whether on our Discord, social media, in the press, or through content creators.[/p][h2]Hell is Us Press Tour[/h2][p]May was a big month for us in terms of meeting with the press and content creators during our North American and European press tours.[/p][p]The North American tour took place at our Rogue Factor offices in the Mile-End district of Montreal. Representatives from both international and local media, as well as content creators, responded to our invitation for a hands-on experience with [i]Hell is Us[/i]![/p][p]We could tell you more, but here’s a video that captures the energy of the event:[/p][p][url="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFb1dLGmJK8"]Hell is Us Press Tour - Rogue Factor, Montréal, Québec[/url]

[/p][previewyoutube="OFb1dLGmJK8;full"][/previewyoutube][p][/p][p]No time to rest! We then packed our bags and headed to [b]Bigben Week[/b] in Paris, France, where European media and content creators got their turn to discover [i]Hell is Us[/i].[/p][p]At this event, our Creative Director and Art Director, Jonathan Jacques Belletête took the time to answer your questions posted on X :

[url="https://x.com/HellisUsGame/status/1929167887182205138/video/1"]Hell is Us (@HELLisUSgame) / X[/url][/p][h2]What did they think of the game?[/h2][p]Here is some of the coverages that the press and content creators published about their hands-on experience of Hell is Us![/p][p]"[i]Hell is Us is my most anticipated game for the rest of the year[/i]" - Greg Miller from Kinda Funny Games.[/p][p][/p][p][dynamiclink href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7LRDO-y9mNI"][/dynamiclink][/p][p][/p][p]"[i]Still, I was very invested in the bizarre, new-weird setting that Rogue Factor has crafted, and it so far has the makings of being one of 2025's more original and creative takes on the action-RPG experience. [/i]" - Alessandro Fillari from IGN[/p][p][url="https://www.ign.com/articles/hell-is-us-brings-a-new-weird-approach-to-the-sci-fi-action-rpg"]Hell is Us Brings a 'New-Weird' Approach to the Sci-Fi Action-RPG - IGN[/url][/p][p]“[i]Hell is Us is a promising confluence of ideas. I enjoy the blend of Zelda-like dungeons, Elden Ring’s sense of discovery, and detective-style investigations and puzzle-solving. (...) Rogue Factor has carefully shaved opaqueness from its intentionally challenging puzzle design. This makes even the simplest problem-solving feel more rewarding[/i].” - Marcus Stewart from Game Informer[/p][p][url="https://www.gameinformer.com/preview/2025/05/30/show-dont-tell"]Hell is Us Preview - Show, Don't Tell - Game Informer[/url][/p][h2]Demo Available right now![/h2][p]Can’t wait to try the game yourself and forge your own opinion? You can! The Hell is Us system requirements feature my biggest pet peeve, upscaling tech. Using upscaling to determine the minimum and recommended hardware to run a game is a major red flag. That being said, there's nothing wrong with using upscaling to improve performance if your gaming PC or laptop is struggling, but it shouldn't be factored in when system requirements are released, as it can be somewhat misleading.

You're going to need one of the best graphics cards from our buying guide to get the best out of Hell is Us, according to these specs. Even then, you can only expect 30fps at 4K with some form of upscaling. While it's no secret that gamers have adopted the likes of Nvidia DLSS as a useful tool to enhance gaming performance, it should not become a crutch for developers to rely on when testing a game for system requirements. notes.title: Meet the main character | Remi
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/c459c1f83ed3956794c087bfa55a9f4967ce270c.jpg[/img]

Remi’s return was never meant to be triumphant. His homeland is a fractured, haunted place—one that never truly let him go. And something lingers in the ruins, waiting.

He was only five years old when his mother smuggled him out of Hadea, a nation closed off from the world. No one was allowed in or out. But she made a choice—one that condemned her son to a life of questions. He understands why she did it. He knows she wanted him to have a better life, beyond the suffocating isolation of Hadea. But that knowledge does nothing to quiet the trauma of having been left behind.
He does not seek justice. He does not seek redemption. He seeks them. The parents who abandoned him. The nation that erased him. He needs to confront them.
Now, decades later, he has finally found his way back.

[h1][b]A Man Defined by What’s Missing[/b][/h1]

Remi grew up in Canada’s foster system, raised by strangers in a land that never truly felt like his own. All he carried from his past were the name of his birthplace—Jova—and the fact that his father was the village blacksmith. That, and a strange necklace he’s always kept with him.

When Remi joined the ON Peacekeeping Forces, it wasn’t out of duty, but as a means to an end. When Hadea plunged into civil war, he saw an opportunity—a chance to cross the border under the guise of a humanitarian mission. As the operation was being shut down, he deserted his post to slip into the country before the window closed.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/4a80e07d2a307b3bb12aa04130192ff3a6f250fc.png[/img]

The land he once belonged to should have been war-torn, divided by conflict. But what he finds is something far worse—something that defies all logic. The civil war he expected has been swallowed by a force he cannot explain. Each step he takes uncovers fragments of a past he was once part of — pieces of a story he was not aware of, now staring back at him through the wreckage. But understanding what happened here comes at a cost, and the deeper he digs, the more he realizes that the truth may be far more terrifying than he ever imagined. Yet, he cannot turn back—he has spent his entire life chasing it.

[h1][b]A World That Demands More Than Survival[/b][/h1]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/0770dd6a51cd46f1363e5d188794979d9bd644cf.png[/img]

The world of Hell is Us is not just a backdrop—it is a test. There are no clear answers, no simple threats, only the brutal demand to adapt or perish.
Remi’s only tools are a set of mysterious weapons—whose origin is as enigmatic as the forces he must face—a resourceful drone named KAPI, and a datapad. They’ll prove useful, but the answers he’s looking for… he’ll have to find on his own.

[h1][b]The Weight of Isolation[/b][/h1]

Remi won’t be handed the answers he seeks. If he wants to understand what happened here, he’ll have to search for clues—scattered across the land, buried in ruins, and hinted at in the words and actions of those he meets. Some may help him, but no one will offer up the truth for free. In these troubled times, everyone has their own burdens, and their willingness to assist may depend on what he can do for them.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/52932bf2441722c8373be7f5b22822966b701237.png[/img]

You must read the world itself—follow the remnants left behind by those who came before, listen for the unnatural silence that signals danger, and decide whether to push forward or turn back. Every discovery is earned, and every mistake is yours alone.
Remi’s journey isn’t just about surviving what lies ahead—it’s about confronting what’s always been missing. The civil war may have reshaped Hadea, but for him, the real wound was inflicted long before the conflict began.

What if the truth he’s been seeking is worse than not knowing?

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/996d0ab79c53ebe64d7d3f44c7d58e4057849e72.png[/img]
 
We’ve only scratched the surface of Remi’s journey. In the coming months, we will reveal more about his past, the dangers he will face, and the choices that will define him.
But in a world where the truth has been buried under centuries of silence, will understanding be enough?

Follow us on our Social Medias and prepare for what lies ahead. The answers are coming—but so is something else.

notes.title: ⚠️ Known technical Issue with some Intel CPUs
notes.content:
Hello everyone,

As we gear up for the Hell is Us demo  (June 2–16), we want to inform you about a technical issue that may affect a small number of players using Intel 13th and 14th Gen CPUs.

[h1][b]🧠 In brief, what’s the Issue?[/b][/h1]

Some recent Intel CPUs (13th and 14th Gen) are experiencing random crashes in games built with Unreal Engine 5, like Hell is Us. The root cause is a hardware instability known as[b] “Vmin Shift”[/b], triggered by high voltage and heat due to overly aggressive motherboard settings.

Intel has identified the issue and is rolling out a BIOS microcode update (version 0x12B) to fix it. However, this update depends on motherboard manufacturers, so it may not yet be available for all systems.

[b]👉 Official Intel resource: [url=https://community.intel.com/t5/Mobile-and-Desktop-Processors/Intel-Core-13th-and-14th-Gen-Desktop-Instability-Root-Cause/m-p/1634305]Intel Community – Vmin Shift Instability[/url][/b]

[h1][b]🎮 Other Major Games Affected[/b][/h1]

This issue isn’t unique to Hell is Us. Several high-profile games have reported similar problems:
[list]
[*] Remnant 2
[*] Path of Titans
[*] Warhammer 40,000: Darktide
[*] Star Wars Jedi: Survivor
[*] Dragonkin : The Banished
[*] Lords of the Fallen
[*] Black Myth : Wukong
[/list]
Some studios have even added in-game warnings for players using these CPUs.

[h1][b]🛠️ What Can You Do?[/b][/h1]
[olist]
[*] Update your BIOS to the latest version from your motherboard manufacturer.
[*] Enable “Intel Baseline” settings in the BIOS if available.
[*] If you're not comfortable with BIOS updates, we recommend contacting a local technician or your motherboard’s support team.
[*] Update the CPU microcode using Intel XTU : https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/download/17881/intel-extreme-tuning-utility-intel-xtu.html
[/olist]
[h1][b]📢 Support During the Demo[/b][/h1]
If you encounter issues during the Steam Next Fest demo, here’s how to reach us:

[list]
[*] Nacon Support: https://my.nacongaming.com/en-US/support
[*] Official Discord: Use the #bugs-report and #feedback channels
[*] Steam: Check the “Known Issues” section on the demo page
[*] Intel Support: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/support.html
[/list]

Thanks to everyone who has helped us identify and troubleshoot these issues. Your feedback is invaluable in making Hell is Us the best experience possible.

🔥 See you in Hadea,
The Hell is Us Team

notes.title: A Closer Look at Ultra Settings and 4K Performance in Hell is Us
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/5ad6e483eb9cc63a2dca13909b837627d6b8bd3a.jpg[/img]

Hey everyone,

Following the recent reveal of the PC specifications for Hell is Us, we've seen a lot of passionate discussion—especially around the mention of 30 FPS in 4K with a RTX 4090 GPU when using Ultra settings. 

Link to PC Specs news :
https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1620730/view/515211349279638277?l=english
 
We’d like to take a moment to clarify what that actually means, and why there’s more to the story than that single number.
 
[h3][b]Understanding Our Graphics Presets[/b][/h3]
The performance estimates we provided are based on very conservative benchmarks. Our Ultra settings aim to push visual fidelity as far as possible—and we do mean ultra.
Here's how our built-in upscaling is configured across each preset:

[b]Low: 50% 
Medium: 40%
High: 30%
Very High: 20%
Ultra: 10%[/b]

By default, the game uses Unreal Engine’s Temporal Super Resolution (TSR) for upscaling, but we also support DLSS, XeSS, and FSR—all of which will be fully updated to their latest versions at launch in September.
 
[h3][b]So... 30 FPS on a 4090?[/b][/h3]
With Ultra settings, we prioritize visual fidelity over framerate. That said, the RTX 4090 will run Hell is Us at higher than 30 FPS in 4K Ultra—but it may not consistently reach 60 FPS. We’re simply being realistic in our communication to avoid overpromising. Our goal is to set clear expectations, not to limit what your system can achieve.
Remember, you’re always free to tune the settings to find the balance that’s right for you. Ultra is just the upper ceiling.
 
[h3][b]Try It for Yourself[/b][/h3]
Don’t let this hold you back from giving the demo a try during the upcoming Steam Next Fest. You’ll be able to test the game directly and get a feel for how it performs on your own system. Every PC is different, and real-world performance can often surprise you.
Thanks again for your feedback and support—we love seeing the community so engaged, and we’re excited for you to dive into the world of Hell is Us.
 
See you soon,
The Hell is Us Team

After introducing the game’s concept, themes, and a first glimpse of gameplay, it’s finally time for the ultimate test: letting you play it.

[u][b]From June 2 to June 16, Hell is Us will be playable via a demo on Steam.[/b][/u]

[h1]🎮 [b]A quick word for our console players:[/b][/h1]

We know many of you are eagerly awaiting the game, and we would have loved to offer the demo on consoles as well. Unfortunately, due to technical constraints, this isn’t currently possible — it’s simply much easier to release a demo on PC.
Please rest assured: Hell is Us will launch simultaneously on PC and consoles, with the same content and the same level of polish. Development is progressing equally across all platforms — this limitation only concerns the demo.

[h1][b]📖 What does the demo cover?[/b][/h1]

The demo begins right at the start of the game.
You’ll step into Rémi’s shoes, armed with only the limited information he has, and begin your descent into Hadea.
This introduction is meant to ease you into Hell is Us and its core gameplay systems.
It won’t show you everything the full game has to offer — it’s just the beginning.
Some of the key elements, like exploration and the player plattering experience, truly come into their own as the world opens up and the layers unfold.

[h1][b]🔧 The game is still in development[/b][/h1]

The full release is set for September 4, nearly three months after the demo goes live.
While the demo represents a solid slice of the game, some features and content will only be available in the final version.

[b]🗣️ Localisation:[/b]

The demo will be available in English only, including full English voice acting.
The full game will support the following languages:

[b]Voice acting[/b]
English, French

[b]Text & Subtitles[/b]
English, French, Italian, German, Spanish, Chinese (Simplified), Russian, Polish, Portuguese, Japanese, Korean, Turkish.

[h1][b]⚔️ Difficulty Options[/b][/h1]

Hell is Us is not designed to be an easy game — but it is designed to be accessible.
The demo includes three difficulty levels as well as several customization options to tailor the experience to your play style.
We encourage you to experiment and find the setting that feels right.


[h1][b]💻 PC Specs[/b][/h1]

If you checked the system requirements earlier on Steam, you might have noticed they seemed a bit high. That’s because we hadn’t completed our full optimization tests yet.
We’ve now finalized the specs, and you can find the updated requirements on our Steam page.
Additionally, we’ll put together a dedicated news post with more details very shortly.


[h1][b]💬 We want your Feedback[/b][/h1]

This demo is our final opportunity to gather your feedback before launch — and we’ll be paying close attention.
You can share your impressions in the Steam Discussions, on social media, or directly on Discord, where we’ll be actively engaging with the community.
We’re also setting up dedicated channels for demo feedback, so don’t hesitate to jump in.

Join our Discord ➡️ [url=https://discord.gg/vKnb5SBJ4a style=button]DISCORD[/url]

[h1][b]👁️ The rest is yours to discover.[/b][/h1]

It wouldn’t be Hell is Us if we told you everything, would it?

We hope you enjoy the demo — and we can’t wait to see how you experience the world of Hell is Us.

CGMagazine was also able to sit down with some of Hell Is Us’ important team members: creative director Jonathan Jacques Belletête, founder and head of Rogue Factor Yves Bordeleau, and audio director Antoine Vachon. notes.title: Hell is Us | Community Update #1
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/99a3c756c38f561d01b2078e88156b60bda644b4.jpg[/img]

Hi everyone, 

Welcome to the very first Hell is Us Community Update! 

With this new format, we want to take a little time—at least once a month—to talk directly to you, as Rogue Factor, the people behind Hell is Us. Not from Hadea (thankfully), but from Montreal. A much calmer place... most of the time.  

Since this is the first edition, we’ll use the opportunity to go a bit beyond just “last month” and do a quick recap of where we’ve come from so far.  

[h2][b]FROM REVEAL TO TRAILERS[/b][/h2]

A lot has happened since our first reveal in April 2022. But let’s not rewind that far. Let’s start somewhere exciting: the two State of Play showcases. 

We were lucky enough to be featured in two of Playstation’s biggest events lately: 

First, with our Gameplay Reveal Trailer, where we introduced the world of Hell is Us — its tone, its world, and a few glimpses of what’s hiding beyond the Border. 

And later, with our Release Date Trailer, which focused more on Remi, the complex human at the center of all this. 

[b]Watch the Gameplay Reveal [/b]

[previewyoutube=ynk7LyKGNHM;full][/previewyoutube]

The goal was simple: give you a sense of what Hell is Us is all about — without showing too much. Because this is a game that’s better felt than explained. That said… we also knew you’d want to see more gameplay. 

[h2][b]EXTENDED GAMEPLAY EXPLAINED[/b][/h2]

So we followed it up with the Extended Gameplay video — a 15-minute walkthrough with our Creative Director and Art Director, Jonathan Jacques-Belletête (that we will call JJB from now on). 

[b]Watch the Extended Gameplay [/b]

[previewyoutube=Q69e1A3ovxI;full][/previewyoutube]

In it, JJB dives deep into a longer sequence that better shows what the game is really like to play — the mood, the pace, the tension, the danger. You responded better than we could’ve hoped, and that gave us even more motivation to keep refining what matters most. 

You also got a first taste of how the game balances two key pillars: Exploration and Combat. In our minds, it’s 50/50 — and the way you navigate between those two will shape your experience. 

Around the same time, we released a blog explaining one of our core philosophies: Player Plattering. 

This one’s close to our hearts. It’s a design idea born from our love for games that lets players figure things out for themselves — games that don’t over-explain, don’t hold your hand, and trust you to create your own meaning. That’s what we’re aiming for with Hell is Us. 

[b][url=https://blog.playstation.com/2024/09/24/hell-is-us-first-gameplay-of-the-ps5-action-adventure-out-2025/]Read the Player Platerring Blog[/url] [/b]

[h2][b]INTRODUCING REMI[/b][/h2]

Then there’s Remi — our protagonist. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/99885b15b16a5b7f22af25466154eaa3a5c495af.jpg[/img]

He’s… complicated. And we like him that way. He’s not a savior, not a chosen one, and definitely not invincible. He’s human. And throughout the game, he’ll evolve. 

We introduced Remi more properly in the Release Date Trailer, and announced he’s voiced by the incredible Elias Toufexis — the one and only voice of Adam Jensen in Deus Ex. It was a reunion with JJB (they’ve got history), and honestly? We can’t imagine anyone else in the role. 

You can follow Elias on X: https://x.com/EliasToufexis 
And yes, more content with him is coming soon!

[b]Release Date Trailer[/b]

[previewyoutube=8iZbNIAM8eQ;full][/previewyoutube]

We’re also working on a dedicated blog about Remi, so you can get a deeper sense of who he is — and who he isn’t. 

[h2][b]INVESTIGATION AT THE HEART OF THE EXPERIENCE[/b][/h2]

Most recently, we released the Investigation Trailer, which focused on an essential part of the game: how you make sense of what’s happening around you. 

We’d shown the world. We’d shown combat. But investigation is where the game opens up — where Player-Plattering really shines. 

Naturally, JJB returned for a 7-minute breakdown of how investigation works, how it connects to the world, and how it avoids feeling like a checklist. 

[b]Watch the Investigation Trailer [/b]

[previewyoutube=dH0oJyvku68;full][/previewyoutube]

[h3][b]What’s Next? [/b][/h3]

If you’ve been following us, a lot of this might already sound familiar. But we’re not here just to recap the past. Here's a peek at what’s next: 

[b]Two upcoming dev blogs[/b] — including the one about Remi. They’ll dive deeper into the world,characters and share some of the thoughts that shaped the project. 

[b]Behind-the-scenes content[/b] — meet more members of the Rogue Factor team, see how things have evolved, and get to know the minds behind the game. 

And of course, we'd love you to follow us on our socials (links at the bottom) not only we will continuously share new content, but we love to discuss theories, make some challenges, and some might make you get your hands so some cool stuff, just saying… 

[h2][b]MAY, A BIG MONTH FOR HELL IS US[/b][/h2]

With some Press and Creators coming to Montreal to have a first experience of Hell is Us, and BigBen Week coming up in Paris in just a week,  we're starting to show the game to more and more people, and things are becoming much more concrete every day.
 
We’re just four months away from release — and things really start to accelerate. 

We couldn’t skip over everything we’ve done so far in this first Community Update, but future editions will focus more on the present: what we’re working on right now, what’s changing, and how the game is shaping up as we head toward launch.  You might even pick up on a few behind-the-scenes secrets along the way.

Thank you again for your continued interest in Hell is Us. Seeing players connect with our vision is what keeps us going every day. 
 
We can’t wait for you to finally get your hands on it. 

Until next time,
— The Hell is Us Team

notes.title: Poll Week | The Path You Chose
notes.content:
[url={STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/b481ac3b709651593cfb9955789c9d6a06657634.png][img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/40689514d0c98b269e78492b6bc3148440ddda19.png[/img][/url]

Hadea is strange. And dangerous.

In just a few months, you’ll walk its scorched soil through Rémi’s footsteps. He chose to be there. He has a purpose.

But what if you didn’t choose?

What if you simply woke up… in the wrong place?

That’s the question we asked you last week on X. And here is the story you told.
________________________________________

You awaken in Hadea, with no memory of how you got there. The sky is unfamiliar. The land is barren, but not dead. A civil war burns in the distance. You don’t belong here. And nothing about this place suggests you’re welcome.

Whoever put you here apparently wanted to give you a chance. Before you lies a choice. Four weapons—each pulsing with a light you don’t recognize, forged from a material you’ve never seen. All meant for close combat.

 [list]
[*] [b]One-handed sword – 40%[/b]
[*]  Two-handed sword – 25.5%
[*]  Double axe – 20.6%
[*]  Polearm – 13.2%
[/list]

You reach for the one-handed sword.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/fd3a3200105f6eb72752924a8f7ee7d002589f04.jpg[/img]

Not because it’s the strongest. But because it feels familiar. In a world that defies everything you know, that’s all you can cling to.

This sword is yours now. It may not be the best. It may not even be enough. But it’s yours.
And with it, you walk.
________________________________________

The land grows stranger. No one crosses your path. No sound but the wind.
And then: a gate. Sealed, ancient, whispering.
No lock. No handle. But four pillars surround it—each one humming in rhythm with your blade. Each marked by an emotion.

Your hand hesitates. Rage pulses in your veins. But something in you leans toward something else. Not joy, exactly. But release.

[list]
[*] [b]Ecstasy – 27%[/b]
[*] Rage – 26.5%
[*] Grief – 24%
[*] Terror – 22.5%
[/list]

Ecstasy.

You strike the pillar. The gate opens.
On the ground: a sword—like yours, but changed. Its shape refined, its light glowing golden. You pick it up. You feel it: not just power… but confidence. A dangerous kind. And yet, welcome.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/7202be885150b95eef4fa59d25d0ac1f79fe8dff.jpg[/img]
________________________________________

This place… it doesn’t feel like any known age. No culture you’ve learned about. You’re walking through the remains of something not meant for you.
Hadea is ancient. Lost. And you’re alone.
Still, you walk.
In the distance: a grand hall. Four corridors.

Another choice. Another test.

Each path promises something. But each is guarded. Not by man, nor beast—but by creatures you can’t explain. Shapes twisted just enough to be wrong.

[list]
[*] [b]Twister humanoid (43.5%)[/b]
[*] Crawling tailed being (16.3%)
[*] Brute with wing-like arms 17.7%
[*] Floating ghostly shape 22.4%
[/list]

You follow your instinct—and face the most human-looking one.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/9fa86817c95ce4c9a8b3cc6d20a43a83765e803f.gif[/img]

It’s a brutal fight. But you survive. Just barely.
Any of the others, and you wouldn’t have. You know it.
In Hadea, instinct is the only thing that hasn’t lied to you yet.
________________________________________

Past the corpse of your enemy, a door awaits. This one is… unlocked.
Even here, sometimes luck exists. Or so you think.
Inside: a word etched into the stone wall—[b]Vigil[/b].
It means nothing to you.

On the table: a key. And four locked chests. Each marked with a word:
Strength. Knowledge. Wealth. Escape.
Your final choice.

[list]
[*]  [b]Knowledge – 53%
[/b][*]  Strength – 28%
[*]  Escape – 13%
[*]  Wealth – 5.6%
[/list]

Surprisingly, this was your clearest decision.

You’re not ready to leave. You don’t crave gold. Power means little without understanding.
You choose to know.
The key turns—but remains stuck in place., sealed, not to be used again.
 
The lid opens.

Inside, a single document:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/b4a7a8c5d4e57bda13f91df40208656faf928fba.png[/img]

What is Jova? No matter what is it, that is your next destination.
________________________________________

You are the first to arrive here in a very long time.

But maybe—just maybe—someone else, coming from outside, looking for answers, will follow your footsteps. Maybe you’ll cross paths and together, find the answer you seek.

Welcome to Hadea.

notes.title: Hell is Us | Welcome to Hadea
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/911481ba5113d19aa538b653ca2654f5b1654c93.png[/img]

Hadea is not just a country, it is a mystery.

A fractured land where the known and the unknown collide, haunted by the aftermath of civil war. For its inhabitants, it is both home and torment — a place that watches in silence as they struggle to survive its relentless trials.

To understand Hadea is to step into the very heart of Hell is Us.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/e2e5a792bb179b7d7a2a3a1291cc2fe856e5d0f4.jpg[/img]

[h1][b]The Allure of a Broken Land.[/b][/h1]

Hadea still pulses with culture and history, its people proud of their homeland. It has always been a harsh place to live, but now, it stands at its lowest — transformed into a realm of desolation and anguish. The skies hang heavy, and the land itself seems to resent those who tread upon it. Yet, even amidst the devastation, Hadea holds a haunting allure. Its remnants of the past offer fleeting glimpses into a forgotten era, while its scarred landscapes invite exploration. From its eerie forests to its silent ruins, Hadea is unlike anywhere else, drawing the curious and the brave to uncover its secrets.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/9cbd55254b538f2b971f9f594e7e5161a1d13da4.jpg[/img]

Hadea does not explain itself. Its ruins, forests, and towns hold remnants of lives erased by the civil war and the events that followed. Monuments crumble in silence, their stories left to the imagination. The land is both a puzzle and a reflection of the past.
Each step forces you to confront truths you might rather leave buried, blurring the line between victim and participant. Hadea compels you to grapple with its mysteries and reckon with your own.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/7ab1812e8de3542cb5ab38e76fe2cb1a11c9c7ed.jpg[/img]

[h1][b]A Test of Will[/b][/h1]

Each step shapes your relationship with the land, whether you seek its truths or simply fight to endure its hostility. The entities that roam its terrain are as enigmatic as the world itself.
Facing them is not just a test of strength but a journey into the very essence of this fractured world. And yet, amid the dangers, Hadea’s tragic beauty persists, urging you to explore its depths and marvel at its singularity.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/fffcce1a590baa2f07ae0cf7e7a970b200cd8237.jpg[/img]

[h1][b]Hadea’s Legacy[/b][/h1]

In Hell is Us, Hadea is more than a setting—it is an active force in your journey. Its treacherous terrain and haunting beauty shape every decision you make, testing your resolve at every turn. The land remembers its pain, its history, and its trespassers. It holds answers, but only for those willing to confront its layers of truth and torment. As you uncover its secrets, you may find that understanding Hadea means understanding yourself.

[h1][b]What Lies Ahead[/b][/h1]

The story of Hadea is far from complete. In the months to come, we will reveal more about its history, its mysteries, and its role in Rémi’s journey. But remember, Hadea does not give up its truths lightly. To walk its paths is to face the unknown—and to marvel at the beauty hidden within its darkness.

notes.title: Hell is Us | Uncover the Unknown
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/73d0c2aeff4ec9218e1fc1d9272456a78b078635.jpg[/img]

Two weeks ago at NACON Connect, we unveiled the Investigation Trailer for Hell is Us, offering a deeper look at how players will navigate the game's world, uncover its secrets, and piece together the mystery that haunts Hadea. If you missed it, now is the perfect time to catch up.

🎥 Watch the Investigation Trailer

https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1620730/view/500567043120038935?l=english

In Hell is Us, survival is not just about combat—it’s about understanding the world around you. Hadea requires you to rely on your instincts, curiosity, and keen observation to make sense of what surrounds you. Cryptic symbols, forgotten ruins, and strange markings scattered throughout Hadea tell a fragmented story, but it’s up to you to interpret their meaning. 

You won’t be entirely alone. The people of Hadea may share knowledge, if you’re willing to listen—and offer your help in return. Throughout your journey, you’ll also encounter unexpected allies. One of them is a mysterious drone that follows you, capable of scanning and analyzing the world, though its purpose—and its origin—remain unknown.

Often, intuition will guide you in the right direction. But Hadea holds secrets layered beneath the surface. Some are meant to stay hidden, and they won’t reveal themselves easily. It’s in those moments that your attention to detail and persistence will make all the difference.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/84f97a22f97449041b774a5eca4db5a5a281b69b.jpg[/img]

Investigation lies at the heart of the Hell is Us experience. In the coming months, we’ll reveal more about the world of Hadea, the enigmatic forces that shape it, and the protagonist’s personal connection to this haunting land.

Until then, watch the trailer again, study every frame, and start piecing together the puzzle—because in Hell is Us, the truth is never handed to you.

notes.title: The sci-fi adventure game from Deus Ex's art director now has Adam Jensen's voice actor, a September release date, and more techno-freak horror vibes than you can shake an augment at
notes.content: I've been kind of jazzed for Hell Is Us since it was announced in 2022, in large part because the project is being headed up by Jonathan Jacques-Belletête—I loved his work as art director on Deus Ex: Human Revolution. (Yes, I am an unrepentant fan of the piss filter.) But then it fell off the radar for a couple years and I forgot about it until a surprise appearance in Sony's 2024 State of Play showcase, with a 2025 release target. And now, thanks to the most recent State of Play, we have a full-on release date: Hell Is Us will be out on September 4... Read more.

notes.title: No Map, No Guide, Just You.
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42249540/ad3dbc24dbbba08be1e590a2a56946a508ba010b.jpg[/img]

In Hell is Us, Player Plattering strips away the maps and waypoints—leaving you to trust nothing but your instincts, the clues you uncover, and the chaos around you.

[b]Jonathan Jacques-Belletete - Executive Creative Director and Art Director of Hell is Us:[/b]

[i]In Hell is Us, you won’t have a magical map or compass revealing all points of interest surrounding you, no markers identifying your next quest objective, and no artificial or mechanical guides to orient you. Instead, we invite you to dive directly into the game’s universe and rely on your own observation, reasoning, and intuition to progress. The environments are not there simply to decorate, they are there to communicate. Correspondingly, paying attention to what the NPCs tell you is crucial; as what they tell you is actual organic information about what to do and how to do it.

We call this concept “Player-Plattering”, as it is the opposite of “Silver-Plattering”. It represents our deliberate choice not to serve everything to the player on a silver platter with ready-made directions and answers. Instead, we want the player to regain full control of their adventure by exploring, discovering, and deciding for themselves.

Although this choice is bold, it aims to create a deeply immersive gameplay experience. You’ll need to explore every corner of our world, pay attention to even the smallest clues, and be creative in solving the investigation that lies ahead. We firmly believe that this approach enhances immersion, plunging you into an adventure where every discovery is the result of your own cognitive effort. We want to bring back the true, old school, joy of exploring and discovering.[/i]

notes.title: After 2 years of silence, Hell is Us makes a surprise reappearance at Sony's State of Play showcase
notes.content: In April 2022, Deus Ex: Human Revolution art director Jonathan Jacques-Belletete unveiled his new project, a third-person descent into awfulness called Hell is Us, in development at Mordheim: City of the Damned studio Rogue Factor. It was supposed to be out sometime in 2023, and obviously that didn't happen—in fact, not much at all has happened on the public-facing front since then. But now it's back, with a 2025 release target and a debut gameplay trailer that appeared at today's State of Play showcase... Read more.

notes.title: Mordheim studio's new game is putting out Annihilation vibes
notes.content:
I can't tell you if Hell Is Us, the newly announced next game from developers Rogue Factor, is actually like the movie Annihilation, because they haven't really shown the game yet. But I can tell you that they're clearly trying to evoke Annihilation vibes, with the trailer channeling that blown-out synth sound and scattering humanlike inhuman mineral figures across the landscape. Annihilation is a good mood to channel. I hope the third-person explore-o-melee game does turn out a bit like that when it arrives in 2023.
